report.source_text: Computed tomography (CT) of the temporal bone revealed a large mass of mixed density with cystic and solid components. It was ill-defined and infiltrative and had an extensively enhancing component extending to the left petrous apex and left side of the clivus. There was an inferior extension to the left infratemporal fossa and nasopharyngeal and parapharyngeal spaces, displacing the nasopharynx anteriorly with adjacent airway narrowing without mucosal invasion. The lesion extended to the left mastoid air cells and middle ear cavity. It infiltrated the left jugular bulb and inferiorly extended to the proximal jugular vein with non-opacification, invasion, and significant osseous destruction of the left petrous bone and occipital condyle. Dehiscence, left carotid canal resorption, and left jugular foramen widening were also observed (Fig. 1, Fig. 2).

This finding likely prompted further vascular imaging, which, according to the known final diagnosis, was a CT angiography that revealed a left dissection aneurysm in the petrous part of the ICA.

The mass infiltrated the left jugular bulb, extended to the proximal jugular vein with non-opacification, and caused significant osseous destruction of the left petrous bone and occipital condyle.
Dehiscence, left carotid canal resorption, and left jugular foramen widening were observed on CT of the temporal bone.
A left dissection aneurysm in the petrous part of the ICA was revealed by diagnostic CT angiography.
